JSON: Name: coarse_to_fine_crackcue Title: Coarse-to-fine reconstruction-based crack cue for robust cross-dataset crack detection Short Hypothesis: Concatenating a coarse-to-fine reconstruction-derived crack cue with the original image as input to a segmentation network increases cross-dataset crack segmentation performance (F1/ODS) compared to the same segmentation network trained and tested without the cue. Related Work: Traditional crack detection methods rely on thresholding, edge operators, frequency-domain filters, or classical classifiers; these approaches lack semantic discrimination and are sensitive to background textures and illumination. Deep learning segmentation models (U-Net and encoder-decoder variants) improve in-dataset accuracy but exhibit limited cross-dataset generalization due to appearance shifts. Recent works use transformer architectures and hybrid CNN-transformer encoders to capture long-range context, and specialized modules (deformable convolutions, multi-scale fusion, orientation-aware detectors) to handle complex crack geometries; however, these methods still rely primarily on raw image features and remain sensitive to contrast changes, shadows, blur, and domain gaps. Methods for robust curvilinear segmentation (e.g., local intensity order transforms) provide contrast-invariant representations but depend on local relative ordering and can fail under noise, shadows, or when cracks are not darker than surroundings. Existing methods do not provide a simple, plug-and-play image-level prior that explicitly isolates thin crack signal from varying backgrounds for downstream segmentation. Abstract: We address limited cross-dataset robustness in automated crack segmentation by introducing a plug-and-play coarse-to-fine crack cue that supplies an explicit, image-level prior for segmentation networks. The method generates a coarse crack-free background via max-pooling and upsampling, refines it with a reconstruction encoder-decoder trained only on background regions, and forms a crack cue as the absolute difference between the input image and the reconstructed background. The cue is concatenated with the original image and fed to an off-the-shelf segmentation network. The main contribution is a lightweight, architecture-agnostic pipeline that emphasizes thin, darker crack responses while attenuating background, contrast, shadow, and blur artifacts. Expected outcomes are consistent improvements in cross-dataset segmentation metrics and robustness to common image perturbations, and practical applicability to other curvilinear structure segmentation tasks such as retinal vessel extraction. Experiments: Datasets: Train on CrackTree260 (resized to 512x512). Cross-dataset test sets: CrackLS315, CRKWH100, Stone331 (all resized to 512x512). Additional domain: train on STARE and test on DRIVE and CHASEDB1 for retinal vessel experiments. Baselines: U-Net, DeepCrack, CrackFormer implemented with identical training schedules. Comparative methods: original baselines (no cue), baselines + LIOT, baselines + median-filter-difference cue, baselines + black-hat-difference cue, baselines + Canny edge cue. Proposed variants: baseline + coarse cue (maxpool upsample diff), baseline + fine cue (coarse-to-fine with reconstruction network), baseline + crackcue (concatenate input and fine cue). Metrics: ODS, OIS, AP, precision, recall, F1 (crack datasets); accuracy, AUC, F1 (retinal). Tolerance: 3-pixel matching tolerance for crack evaluation. Training setup: joint training of reconstruction and segmentation networks, batch size 4, 700 epochs, Adam optimizer with lr=1e-4, input size 512x512, max-pool kernel sizes tested {4,8,12}, dilated ground-truth widths d tested {2,3,4,5}, loss balancing lambda values tested {0.25,1,4}. Reconstruction network: encoder-decoder without skip connections, 10 conv layers each. Ablation studies: (1) coarse vs fine cue vs no cue; (2) comparison to LIOT and other cue-generation variants; (3) max-pool kernel size sweep; (4) dilated GT width sweep; (5) lambda sensitivity; (6) runtime impact (FPS) on NVIDIA RTX3090. Robustness tests: apply common corruptions per standardized protocol (defocus blur and low-contrast perturbations) and measure metric degradation with and without cues. Statistical reporting: report mean and standard deviation over 3 independent runs per condition; compute relative percent change vs baseline. Evaluation protocol: use identical post-processing (sigmoid normalization) and threshold sweep to compute PR curves and AP; report ODS and OIS derived from PR curve. For retinal experiments use same training hyperparameters and report Acc/AUC/F1 on evaluation sets. Risk Factors and Limitations: Dependence on crack visual assumptions: the approach assumes cracks are thinner and darker than their surroundings; it may fail for very wide cracks, bright cracks, or cracks with intensity close to background. Reconstruction leakage: the reconstruction network could inadvertently reconstruct or preserve crack-like patterns if annotations are incomplete or dilation is insufficient, reducing cue contrast. Annotation and domain bias: training on a single dataset (CrackTree260) can embed dataset-specific textures and sampling bias; evaluation datasets with differing masks or excluded regions (e.g., Stone331) may skew results. Sensitivity to hyperparameters: max-pool kernel size, dilation width, and loss balance affect cue quality; suboptimal choices can produce false positives. Perturbation regimes not covered: extreme noise types (salt-and-pepper, heavy non-Gaussian noise), specular highlights, or severe geometric distortions may still break cue reliability. Computational cost and latency: generating the fine cue requires an additional reconstruction network at inference, increasing memory use and reducing FPS, which may limit real-time deployment on edge devices. Generalization limits: the method targets thin curvilinear structures and may not transfer to non-curvilinear defects or to modalities where intensity relationships differ (e.g., thermal imagery) without retraining or adaptation.
